edits.new: Back from the meeting at Mianchi, Lin Xiangru was made shangqing for his service and ranked above Lian Po, a general whose merit lay in cities stormed and battles won. Lian Po would not swallow it and swore he would humiliate him wherever they met. Lin Xiangru kept giving ground, until even his own retainers threatened to walk out. The standoff ended with Lian Po baring his back and carrying a bundle of thorns to beg forgiveness; and Lian Po's grievance had had grounds from the start.

edits.new: Before the meeting at Mianchi the king of Zhao, afraid of Qin, did not want to go. Lian Po and Lin Xiangru took counsel and told him that staying away would show Zhao weak and afraid. So the king went, and Lin Xiangru with him. Lian Po escorted him to the border and, taking leave, made an arrangement: allow for the road and the formalities of the meeting, and the round trip should take no more than thirty days; if the king was not back in thirty days, let the crown prince be set up as king, to cut off Qin's hopes. The king agreed. At Mianchi the king of Qin, to the end of the banquet, could not gain the upper hand over Zhao; Zhao, for its part, had massed its forces to meet Qin, and Qin dared not move.

edits.new: Lin Xiangru came back from the meeting at Mianchi and was made shangqing, the highest ministerial rank, placed above Lian Po. Lian Po was Zhao's finest general: he had beaten Qi, taken Yangjin and won a name for courage among the states. His reaction was blunt. Lin Xiangru had earned his place with nothing but his tongue; why should he sit above me? He announced that the next time they met he would humiliate the man. What makes the episode hard is that the grievance had grounds. Lian Po really had great merit from storming cities and fighting in the field, while Lin Xiangru's credit was entered under words. Now both held the top rank at court: one meant to humiliate, the other hid.
edits.reason: English tightened toward parity (Chinese ~9 min, English was ~14).

edits.new: In King Huiwen's time Zhao acquired the Heshi jade from Chu, and King Zhaoxiang of Qin wrote offering fifteen cities for it. The king of Zhao consulted his great general Lian Po and the other ministers, and both answers looked bad: hand it over and the cities might never come, leaving Zhao cheated; refuse, and Qin's armies might. Nothing was settled, and there was no one fit to carry the reply to Qin. Miao Xian put forward Lin Xiangru, and told a story against himself. He had once been guilty of an offence and meant to flee to Yan. Lin Xiangru stopped him: Zhao was strong and Yan weak, and the king of Yan had courted Miao Xian only because he stood in the king of Zhao's favour; flee there, and Yan would tie him up and send him back. Better to "strip and lie on the block", as the phrase went, and ask pardon. Miao Xian did, and the king pardoned him.
edits.reason: Parity: the English retold dialogue (the handclasp at the border) that the Chinese only summarises; tightened.

edits.new: At the Qin court the king received Lin Xiangru in the Zhang Terrace, was delighted with the jade, and passed it around to his ladies and attendants, who all cried long life to him. Lin Xiangru saw he had no intention of paying. He said the gem had a small flaw he would point out, took it back, and stood holding it with his eyes on a pillar, ready to smash it. The alarmed king apologised, sent for the official in charge of maps and pointed out fifteen cities for Zhao. Lin Xiangru judged this mere show. The Heshi jade was a treasure the whole world talked of, he said; the king of Zhao had fasted five days before sending it, and the king of Qin should fast five days and hold the nine-fold ceremony at court before he would dare present it. The king agreed and lodged him at the Guangcheng hostel. Sure that the king would break his word even after fasting, Lin Xiangru had a follower put on coarse clothes, hide the jade in his robe and take it home to Zhao by back roads. At the next audience he laid it out: in more than twenty reigns since Duke Mu, Qin had never kept a firm agreement; the jade was already back in Zhao; "I know that deceiving Your Majesty is a crime deserving death, and I ask to go to the cauldron." The king and his ministers looked at one another. Some attendants moved to drag him out, but the king reasoned that killing him would not bring back the jade and would end good relations with Zhao. In the end he received Lin Xiangru at court with full ceremony and sent him home.
edits.reason: Tightened for parity; the quoted line is a translation of 臣知欺大王之罪當誅，臣請就湯鑊.

edits.new: Within the same biography the gesture of admitting fault appears twice. Lin Xiangru's advice to Miao Xian was to strip and lie on the block to ask pardon; when Lian Po came to the gate, he came stripped to the waist with thorns on his back. Both are postures of baring the body and handing it over. One cannot say that Lian Po knew of the earlier case or was influenced by it; the parallel is the author's observation, not something the text states. Advising the king of Zhao before the mission, Lin Xiangru used a different grammar: first settle where the wrong will lie, with Zhao or with Qin, arrange for it to fall on the other side, and only then decide how far to give. The Grand Historian's verdict: he stepped back and yielded to Lian Po, and his name came to weigh as much as Mount Tai.

One apology did not remake Lian Po's temper. When King Xiaocheng of Zhao died, his successor King Daoxiang sent Le Cheng to replace Lian Po; Lian Po attacked Le Cheng, who fled, and then went over to Daliang in Wei. Earlier, when he had lost power, his retainers had all left, and when he was made a general again they came back; one of them told him that the world deals "the way the marketplace does": people come when you have power and leave when you do not. None of this is a moral verdict on anyone. It only shows that the apology at Lin Xiangru's gate was real, and that it did not rewrite the man from that day on.
edits.reason: Parity: the English retold the retainers' exchange in full; Chinese summarises it.
